tool.name: FastAPI
tool.tagline: Fast, type-hint driven Python framework for building HTTP APIs
tool.description: FastAPI is a modern Python web framework for building APIs, built on Starlette for the web layer and Pydantic for data validation. You declare endpoints as typed functions and get request parsing, validation, JSON serialization and interactive OpenAPI docs from the same code. It is one of the most popular choices for Python back ends, microservices and ML model serving.

concepts.name: What FastAPI is and your first app
concepts.summary: Install FastAPI, write a five-line app and serve JSON over HTTP with the fastapi dev command.
concepts.why: Everything else in FastAPI builds on this loop: write a function, decorate it, run the server, call the URL.
concepts.body:
**FastAPI** is a Python web framework for building HTTP APIs. You write ordinary functions with type hints, and FastAPI uses those hints to parse and validate incoming data, convert your return values to JSON and generate API documentation, all from the same declaration. It stands on two libraries: **Starlette** does the web part (routing, requests, responses, WebSockets) and **Pydantic** does data validation and serialization.

FastAPI is an **ASGI** application, so it doesn't listen on a port by itself; an ASGI server such as Uvicorn runs it. Install it in a virtual environment with the `standard` extras, which bring Uvicorn, the `fastapi` command and common optional packages:

```bash
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install "fastapi[standard]"
```

Save the example as `main.py` and run `fastapi dev main.py` (plain `fastapi dev` also finds a `main.py` with an `app` in it). The development server starts on `http://127.0.0.1:8000`, watches your files and reloads on every save. Open `http://127.0.0.1:8000/` and you get `{"message":"Hello World"}`.

For production use `fastapi run main.py`: no auto-reload, and it listens on `0.0.0.0` so it's reachable from outside the machine or container. Both commands wrap Uvicorn; the equivalent you'll see in older tutorials is `uvicorn main:app --reload`, where `main:app` means "the object `app` in module `main`".

Three things to notice in the code. `app = FastAPI()` creates the application object. `@app.get("/")` registers the function below it for GET requests to `/`. And returning a `dict` is enough: FastAPI turns it into a JSON response with the right `Content-Type`.
takeaways: FastAPI = Starlette for the web layer + Pydantic for data, driven by your type hints
pip install "fastapi[standard]" gives you Uvicorn and the fastapi command
fastapi dev for development (auto-reload), fastapi run for production
Returning a dict, list or model produces a JSON response
pitfalls: Naming your own file fastapi.py: it shadows the real package and the import fails.
Running fastapi dev (auto-reload, localhost only) in production.

quiz.q: Which library does FastAPI rely on to validate request data and serialize responses?
quiz.explain: Pydantic handles data validation and serialization; Starlette handles the HTTP layer and Uvicorn is the server.

quiz.q: Compared with fastapi dev, what does fastapi run main.py change?
options: It runs the app without any ASGI server
It turns off auto-reload and listens on 0.0.0.0
It enables auto-reload and binds to localhost only
quiz.explain: fastapi run is the production mode: no file watching, and it listens on all interfaces.

concepts.name: Path operations and HTTP methods
concepts.summary: Map URL paths and HTTP methods to Python functions with @app.get, @app.post and the other method decorators.
concepts.why: Path operations are the unit of every FastAPI API, and choosing the right method and path is basic API design.
concepts.body:
In FastAPI's vocabulary a **path** is the URL part after the host (`/items/5`), an **operation** is the HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE), and a **path operation** is the pair, handled by a *path operation function*. You declare one with a decorator named after the method: `@app.get`, `@app.post`, `@app.put`, `@app.patch`, `@app.delete` (plus `head`, `options` and `trace`).

Use methods for their HTTP meaning, because browsers, proxies, caches and client libraries rely on it:

- GET reads and must not change anything; it may be cached and retried.
- POST creates something or triggers an action.
- PUT replaces a resource; PATCH updates part of it.
- DELETE removes it.

One path can have several operations: `GET /items` lists, `POST /items` creates. If no route matches the path, the client gets 404; if the path exists but not for that method, 405 Method Not Allowed. Routes are checked **in the order you declare them**, which matters when a fixed path like `/users/me` overlaps a parametrized one like `/users/{user_id}`: declare the fixed one first.

The function may be `def` or `async def`. Start with plain `def`; FastAPI runs it in a thread pool so slow code doesn't block the server (the async lesson explains when to switch). Whatever you return, a dict, list, string, number or Pydantic model, is converted to JSON.

Decorator arguments configure the operation: `status_code=201`, `tags=["items"]` to group it in the docs, `summary=...`, `deprecated=True`. The function's docstring becomes the operation's description in the documentation.

The example uses `TestClient`, which sends requests to the app in-process with no server; the testing lesson covers it properly.
concepts.code:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

app = FastAPI()
items = ["apple", "pear"]

@app.get("/items", tags=["items"])
def list_items():
    """Return every item."""
    return items

@app.post("/items", status_code=201, tags=["items"])
def add_item():
    items.append("plum")
    return {"count": len(items)}

client = TestClient(app)
print(client.get("/items").json())         # ['apple', 'pear']
print(client.post("/items").status_code)   # 201
print(client.put("/items").status_code)    # 405: no PUT for /items
print(client.get("/nope").status_code)     # 404
takeaways: A path operation = path + HTTP method + the function that handles it
Use GET for reads only; POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE for changes
Routes match in declaration order: put fixed paths before parametrized ones
Unknown path gives 404, known path with the wrong method gives 405
pitfalls: Changing data in a GET handler: crawlers, prefetchers and retries will trigger it.

quiz.q: A client sends PUT /items, but only GET and POST are declared for /items. What status code comes back?
quiz.explain: The path exists but not for that method, so FastAPI answers 405.

quiz.q: You declared @app.get('/users/{user_id}') before @app.get('/users/me'), with user_id: int. What happens on GET /users/me?
options: The first route matches and 'me' fails int validation, giving a 422
The /users/me function runs because exact matches always win
FastAPI refuses to start because the routes overlap
quiz.explain: Routes are tried in order, so /users/{user_id} captures 'me' first; declare /users/me before it.

concepts.name: Interactive API docs: /docs and /redoc
concepts.summary: Every app serves an OpenAPI schema plus Swagger UI and ReDoc pages generated from your code.
concepts.why: You get accurate, always up-to-date documentation and a test console for free, for you, your front end team and API clients.
concepts.body:
FastAPI builds an **OpenAPI** description of your API from the path operations, parameters, models and type hints you declare. OpenAPI is the standard JSON format for describing HTTP APIs, and three URLs expose it out of the box:

- `/docs`: **Swagger UI**, an interactive page where you expand an operation, fill in its parameters and press "Try it out" to send a real request.
- `/redoc`: **ReDoc**, a clean read-only reference.
- `/openapi.json`: the raw schema the two pages are built from.

Because the docs are generated from the same declarations FastAPI uses to validate requests, they can't drift out of date: add a query parameter or change a model field and the docs change on the next reload.

The schema is useful beyond the browser. Generators such as openapi-generator or openapi-ts produce typed client SDKs (TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift and more) from `/openapi.json`, and teams diff it between releases to catch breaking changes.

Enrich it cheaply as you go:

- pass `title`, `version` and `description` (Markdown allowed) to `FastAPI(...)`,
- group operations with `tags=[...]`,
- write docstrings, or pass `summary` and `description` to the decorator,
- describe model fields; their descriptions and examples appear in the schema.

To move or remove the pages, pass `docs_url`, `redoc_url` or `openapi_url` to `FastAPI()`; `None` disables one. `openapi_url=None` disables all three, since the UIs load the schema from it. Some teams switch the docs off in production, but hiding them isn't security: protect endpoints with real authentication.
concepts.code:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

app = FastAPI(
    title="Inventory API",
    version="1.2.0",
    description="Manage **items** in the warehouse.",
)

@app.get("/items", tags=["items"], summary="List items")
def list_items():
    """Returns all items, newest first."""
    return []

schema = TestClient(app).get("/openapi.json").json()
print(schema["info"]["title"])     # Inventory API
print(list(schema["paths"]))       # ['/items']
print(schema["paths"]["/items"]["get"]["description"])
# Returns all items, newest first.

# With `fastapi dev` running, open http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs and /redoc
takeaways: /docs (Swagger UI), /redoc (ReDoc) and /openapi.json come for free
Docs are generated from the same declarations used for validation, so they stay accurate
Titles, tags, summaries, docstrings and field descriptions all flow into the schema
docs_url, redoc_url and openapi_url move or disable the pages
pitfalls: Treating disabled docs as protection: the endpoints are still reachable without auth.

quiz.q: Why do FastAPI's docs stay in sync with the code?
options: FastAPI compares the docs to the code at startup and warns on drift
A CI step regenerates them on each commit
They're generated at runtime from the same type hints and models used for validation
Swagger UI scans your source files
quiz.explain: There is only one source of truth: the declarations that also drive parsing and validation.

quiz.q: You create the app with FastAPI(openapi_url=None). What happens?
options: Only /openapi.json disappears; /docs keeps working from a cached copy
quiz.explain: The UIs need the schema, so removing the schema URL disables all three.

concepts.name: Path parameters
concepts.summary: Capture parts of the URL like /items/{item_id} as typed function arguments that FastAPI converts and validates.
concepts.why: Resource URLs such as /users/42 are the backbone of REST APIs, and typed parameters make them safe to use.
concepts.body:
Put a name in braces in the path and give the function a parameter with the same name: `@app.get("/items/{item_id}")` with `def read_item(item_id: int)`. FastAPI extracts that URL segment, and the **type hint** decides what happens next:

- For `/items/42`, the string `"42"` is converted, so `item_id` is the int `42`.
- For `/items/abc`, conversion fails and the client gets a **422** response whose JSON body says which parameter was wrong and why. Your function never runs.

This is the central FastAPI idea: the type hint is documentation, parsing and validation in one. `int`, `float`, `str`, `bool`, `UUID`, `date` and `datetime` all work out of the box.

When only a fixed set of values is valid, use an `Enum` that also subclasses `str`. FastAPI validates against the members, the docs show a dropdown, and your function receives the enum member, so compare with `Color.red` or read `.value`.

Path parameters are always required: a URL either has the segment or it matches a different route. A segment can't contain `/`, unless you use the `path` converter, `{file_path:path}`, which matches the rest of the URL including slashes.

Two practical notes. First, route order: with `/users/me` and `/users/{user_id}`, declare `/users/me` first or `me` is captured as a user id. Second, Pydantic's default conversion is lenient where it's unambiguous (`"007"` becomes `7`) but strict about losing information: `"3.5"` is rejected for an `int` rather than truncated.
takeaways: {name} in the path + a parameter with the same name = path parameter
The type hint converts the value; invalid input gets a 422 before your code runs
Use a str Enum to restrict a parameter to fixed values
{name:path} captures the rest of the URL including slashes
pitfalls: Declaring /users/{user_id} before /users/me, so 'me' never reaches its own route.

quiz.q: With def read_item(item_id: int), what does GET /items/007 pass as item_id?
options: Nothing: a 422 because of the leading zeros
quiz.explain: The segment is a string and Pydantic converts '007' to the int 7.

quiz.q: What does GET /items/3.5 return for item_id: int?
quiz.explain: Pydantic refuses to drop the fractional part, so the request fails validation.

concepts.name: Query parameters
concepts.summary: Function parameters that aren't in the path become query parameters like ?skip=0&limit=10: typed, optional or required.
concepts.why: Filtering, pagination, sorting and search options all travel as query parameters.
concepts.body:
Any function parameter that isn't in the path and has a simple type (int, str, bool, float, enum...) is read from the **query string**, the `?key=value&key2=value2` part of the URL. Types work exactly as for path parameters: values arrive as strings and are converted and validated.

Whether a query parameter is required depends only on its default:

- `limit: int = 10` is optional; when it's missing you get 10.
- `q: str | None = None` is optional; when it's missing you get `None`, so test with `if q is not None`.
- `status: str` with no default is required; leaving it out gives a 422.

Booleans are deliberately forgiving: `true`, `1`, `yes` and `on` mean True; `false`, `0`, `no` and `off` mean False (case-insensitive). Anything else is a 422.

Path and query parameters mix freely, and the order of function parameters doesn't matter: FastAPI identifies each one by name. A name that appears in the path template is a path parameter; any other simple-typed parameter is a query parameter.

Lists are the one surprise. To accept a repeated key such as `?tag=a&tag=b`, write `tag: Annotated[list[str], Query()] = []`. Without `Query()`, FastAPI would assume a list parameter is part of a JSON request body. `Query()` also adds constraints like `max_length`, which the validation lesson covers.

Keep query parameters for things that select or shape a response (filters, pagination, sort order), not for data you're creating; that belongs in the request body.
takeaways: Simple-typed parameters not in the path come from the query string
No default = required; a default (often None) = optional
bool accepts true/false, 1/0, yes/no, on/off
Repeated keys need Annotated[list[str], Query()]
pitfalls: Writing q: str = None: it works but lies about the type; use str | None = None.

quiz.q: For def search(q: str, page: int = 1), what does GET /search?page=2 return?
options: Results with q set to None
A 422 error because q is required
quiz.explain: q has no default, so it's a required query parameter and its absence fails validation.

quiz.q: GET /items?active=off reaches active: bool = True. What value does active have?
options: True, because any non-empty string is truthy
quiz.explain: FastAPI's bool parsing understands off/no/0/false as False.

concepts.name: Request bodies with Pydantic models
concepts.summary: Declare a Pydantic BaseModel parameter and FastAPI reads, validates and parses the JSON request body into it.
concepts.why: Creating and updating resources means accepting structured JSON safely, and models make that declarative.
concepts.body:
To accept JSON in a POST, PUT or PATCH, describe its shape as a **Pydantic model**: a class inheriting from `BaseModel` whose annotated attributes are its fields. Use the model as a parameter type and FastAPI will read the body as JSON, validate it (types, required fields, nested models), hand your function a model instance with attributes like `item.price`, and describe it as a JSON Schema in the docs.

So FastAPI decides where each parameter comes from like this: names in the path are path parameters, simple types are query parameters, Pydantic models are the body. Model fields follow the familiar default rules: no default means required, `str | None = None` means optional.

Pydantic's default **lax mode** converts compatible input, so the JSON string `"3"` for an `int` field becomes 3, and rejects what can't be converted, such as `"abc"` for a float. Failures produce a 422 whose `detail` is a list of errors; each has a `loc` such as `["body", "price"]`, a `msg` and a `type`, so clients can point at the exact field. Extra keys the model doesn't define are ignored by default; set `model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")` to reject them instead.

Models nest naturally: a field can be another model, `list[Tag]` or `dict[str, int]`. To get plain data back, use the Pydantic v2 methods `item.model_dump()` (a dict) or `item.model_dump_json()`. The v1 names `.dict()` and `.json()` are deprecated. For partial updates, `item.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)` returns only the fields the client actually sent.

If a function has two model parameters, FastAPI expects a JSON object with one key per parameter name: `{"item": {...}, "user": {...}}`.
takeaways: A BaseModel parameter = JSON request body, validated and parsed
Path names are path params, simple types are query params, models are the body
Validation errors are 422s with a precise loc for each failing field
Use model_dump() / model_dump_json() in Pydantic v2, not .dict() / .json()
pitfalls: Sending form data or a query string when the endpoint expects JSON: the body must be application/json.

quiz.q: In def update(item_id: int, item: Item, q: str | None = None), where does FastAPI read item from?
quiz.explain: Pydantic model parameters are read from the request body.

quiz.q: A client sends {"name": "Pen", "price": 2, "color": "red"} to a model with only name and price. What happens by default?
options: color is added to the instance as an extra attribute
quiz.explain: Pydantic ignores unknown keys by default; extra='forbid' turns them into errors.

concepts.name: Response models and status codes
concepts.summary: Use return type annotations or response_model to shape, filter and document what an endpoint sends back.
concepts.why: Response models stop you from leaking fields like password hashes and give clients a documented, stable contract.
concepts.body:
FastAPI validates what comes in, and a **response model** controls what goes out. The simplest way is a return type annotation: `def create_user(...) -> UserPublic`. FastAPI validates the return value against `UserPublic`, **filters** it down to that model's fields, serializes it to JSON and documents the response schema.

Filtering is the important part. A common pattern is one model per direction:

- `UserCreate`: what the client sends (includes `password`).
- `UserPublic`: what the client sees (no secrets).
- `UserInDB`: what you store (includes `hashed_password`).

Inherit them from a shared base to avoid repetition. If the function returns a `UserInDB` but is annotated `-> UserPublic`, `hashed_password` is dropped from the response.

When the annotation would be wrong for the type checker, for example you return a dict or an ORM object but want the model in the docs, put it on the decorator instead: `@app.get("/users/{id}", response_model=UserPublic)`. `response_model` takes priority over the annotation, and `response_model=None` turns the feature off. `response_model_exclude_unset=True` omits fields that were never set, which keeps sparse resources compact.

Set the success **status code** on the decorator: `status_code=201` when creating, `204` for an empty "deleted" response. The constants in `fastapi.status` (`status.HTTP_201_CREATED`) read better than bare numbers.

If your return value doesn't fit the response model, that's a bug on the server side, so FastAPI raises an error and the client gets a 500, not a 422. It's a useful safety net: a broken query can't silently ship malformed data.
takeaways: A return annotation or response_model validates, filters and documents the output
Use separate input, output and storage models so secrets never leave the server
response_model= on the decorator wins over the return annotation
Set success codes with status_code=, e.g. 201 for creation
pitfalls: Using the same model for input and output, so clients can set server-owned fields like id or see internal ones.

quiz.q: The function is annotated -> UserPublic but returns a UserInDB that has hashed_password. What does the client receive?
quiz.explain: FastAPI serializes using the declared response model, which filters out extra fields.

quiz.q: Your endpoint returns a value that doesn't match its response model. What does the client get?
options: A 500, because it's a server-side bug
quiz.explain: Response validation failures are the server's fault, so FastAPI responds with an internal server error.

concepts.name: Validation with Annotated, Query, Path and Field
concepts.summary: Add constraints like max_length, ge/le and regex patterns to parameters and model fields with Annotated metadata.
concepts.why: Rejecting bad input at the edge, with clear 422 errors and documented limits, beats hand-written checks in every endpoint.
concepts.body:
Type hints say what type a value is; constraints say which values are acceptable. The modern FastAPI style puts constraints in `typing.Annotated`: `q: Annotated[str | None, Query(max_length=50)] = None`. The first argument is the real type, the rest is metadata FastAPI reads, and the default stays an ordinary Python default.

The parameter functions say where a value comes from and carry its constraints:

- `Query()`, `Path()`, `Header()`, `Cookie()` for parameters, `Body()` for extra values in the body.
- Strings: `min_length`, `max_length`, `pattern` (a regular expression).
- Numbers: `gt`, `ge`, `lt`, `le`, `multiple_of`.
- Documentation and naming: `title`, `description`, `examples`, `alias` (accept `item-query` in the URL), `deprecated=True`.

Inside Pydantic models, `Field()` takes the same constraint names: `price: float = Field(gt=0)`. For rules that need code, write a `@field_validator` for one field or a `@model_validator(mode="after")` for cross-field rules like "end must be after start". Raise `ValueError` with a clear message and Pydantic turns it into a 422 entry for the client.

Since FastAPI 0.115 you can group query parameters into a model: `filters: Annotated[FilterParams, Query()]`. It's a neat way to share pagination or search parameters, and with `model_config = {"extra": "forbid"}` unknown query keys are rejected.

Prefer `Annotated` over the older `q: str = Query(None, max_length=50)` form. Both work, but `Annotated` keeps defaults honest, lets the function be called normally in tests, and enables reusable aliases such as `ItemId = Annotated[int, Path(gt=0)]` shared across many endpoints.
takeaways: Annotated[type, Query(...)/Path(...)/Body(...)] attaches constraints and docs
Field() puts the same constraints on model fields
field_validator and model_validator handle rules that need code; raise ValueError
Reusable aliases like ItemId = Annotated[int, Path(gt=0)] keep endpoints consistent
pitfalls: Validating in the endpoint and returning 400 by hand, so the rule never shows up in the docs or the standard 422 format.

quiz.q: Which is the recommended way to limit an optional query parameter q to 50 characters?
quiz.explain: Annotated carries the Query metadata while the default stays a plain Python default.

quiz.q: A body model needs the rule 'end_date must be after start_date'. What's the best tool?
quiz.explain: Cross-field rules belong in a model validator, which reports them as normal 422 errors.

concepts.name: Errors: HTTPException and exception handlers
concepts.summary: Raise HTTPException for expected failures, and register exception handlers that turn your own exceptions into responses.
concepts.why: Clients need consistent, meaningful error responses, and handlers keep the HTTP mapping out of business logic.
concepts.body:
To stop a request with an error, **raise** `HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Item not found")`. Raise it rather than return it: it unwinds through helper functions and dependencies, and FastAPI turns it into a JSON response `{"detail": "Item not found"}` with that status. `detail` can be any JSON-serializable value, and `headers={...}` adds response headers.

Pick codes by meaning: 400 for a bad request the validators couldn't catch, 401 when the caller isn't authenticated, 403 when they are but aren't allowed, 404 for a missing resource, 409 for a conflict such as a duplicate email. FastAPI already sends 422 for validation failures, and any unhandled exception becomes a 500 and is logged.

Don't sprinkle HTTP into your service layer, though. Define domain exceptions (`class OutOfStock(Exception)`) and register a handler with `@app.exception_handler(OutOfStock)`. The handler receives the request and the exception and returns a response, usually a `JSONResponse`. Now any code that raises `OutOfStock` during a request, however deep, produces that response. Handlers match by class including subclasses, so one handler for a base `AppError` can cover a whole hierarchy.

You can also override the built-in handlers:

- A handler for `RequestValidationError` changes the format of 422 responses; `exc.errors()` gives the error list.
- A handler for `starlette.exceptions.HTTPException` catches both your `HTTPException`s and Starlette's own 404 and 405 responses.
- To keep the default behaviour but add logging, call `fastapi.exception_handlers.http_exception_handler` from your handler.

Keep error bodies consistent across the API; clients write their error handling once.
takeaways: raise HTTPException(status_code, detail) stops the request from any depth
401 = not authenticated, 403 = not allowed, 404 = missing, 409 = conflict
Map domain exceptions to responses with @app.exception_handler
Override RequestValidationError's handler to change the 422 format
pitfalls: Returning HTTPException instead of raising it: FastAPI then tries to serialize the exception object as a normal response.

quiz.q: Why is raising HTTPException better than returning an error dict from a helper function?
options: Raising stops execution from any depth, including helpers and dependencies, and FastAPI builds the error response
Returned dicts can't have a status code
quiz.explain: The exception unwinds the call stack so callers don't have to check return values.

quiz.q: You register a handler for RequestValidationError. What changes?
options: Pydantic stops raising errors in your own code
The response sent when request data fails validation
quiz.explain: That handler produces the response for invalid requests, normally the standard 422.

concepts.name: Dependency injection with Depends
concepts.summary: Declare shared logic such as auth, pagination or DB sessions as functions, and let FastAPI call them and inject the results.
concepts.why: Dependencies are FastAPI's main tool for reuse and for test seams, and they keep endpoints thin.
concepts.body:
A **dependency** is any callable whose result your endpoint needs. Declare it with `Depends`: `page: Annotated[dict, Depends(pagination)]`. For each request FastAPI calls `pagination` first, supplying whatever *it* declares (query parameters, headers, other dependencies), and passes the return value in. The endpoint never calls it and doesn't care where the values came from.

Dependencies use the full parameter system: their inputs are validated, they appear in the docs, and they can raise `HTTPException` to stop the request. That's exactly how authentication checks are built.

The idiomatic pattern is a reusable type alias:

```python
CurrentUser = Annotated[User, Depends(get_current_user)]

def read_me(user: CurrentUser): ...
```

Properties worth knowing:

- **Sub-dependencies**: dependencies can depend on other dependencies, and FastAPI resolves the whole graph.
- **Per-request caching**: if several dependencies need the same one, it runs once per request and the value is shared. `Depends(fn, use_cache=False)` opts out.
- **Classes work** because they're callable: `Depends(Pagination)` builds an instance from query parameters.
- **Side-effect only**: `dependencies=[Depends(verify_key)]` on a decorator runs a check without injecting anything. `APIRouter(...)` and `FastAPI(...)` accept `dependencies=` too, applying them to every route.
- `def` and `async def` dependencies mix freely.

Dependencies are also your testing seam: `app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = fake_db` swaps an implementation for tests without touching endpoint code.
takeaways: Annotated[T, Depends(fn)] runs fn per request and injects its result
Dependencies take parameters and other dependencies, forming a graph
A dependency used several times in one request runs once (cached)
dependencies=[...] on routes, routers or the app runs checks without injecting values
pitfalls: Calling the dependency yourself (Depends(get_db())) instead of passing the function (Depends(get_db)).

quiz.q: Two dependencies in one request both depend on get_settings. How many times does get_settings run?
options: Zero, only direct dependencies of the endpoint run
Once; its value is cached for the rest of the request
quiz.explain: FastAPI caches dependency results per request unless use_cache=False.

quiz.q: You need a dependency that only verifies an API key and returns nothing useful. What's the cleanest declaration?
options: Calling verify_key() at the top of each function
dependencies=[Depends(verify_key)] on the decorator, router or app
quiz.explain: The dependencies list runs the callable without passing its value to the endpoint.

concepts.name: APIRouter and project structure
concepts.summary: Split a growing app into one router per feature, and include them with prefixes, tags and shared dependencies.
concepts.why: A single main.py stops scaling after a few dozen endpoints; routers give you modules a team can work in.
concepts.body:
An `APIRouter` is a mini-app: it has the same `.get`, `.post` and other decorators, and is attached to the real app with `app.include_router(router)`. Give each feature its own module and router:

```text
app/
  main.py          # creates FastAPI(), includes routers
  dependencies.py  # get_session, get_current_user...
  models.py        # Pydantic / SQLModel models
  routers/
    items.py
    users.py
```

A router can carry configuration for all its routes: `APIRouter(prefix="/items", tags=["items"], dependencies=[Depends(get_current_user)], responses={404: {"description": "Not found"}})`. Inside it, paths are relative: `@router.get("/{item_id}")` serves `/items/{item_id}`.

The same options can be passed when including instead: `app.include_router(admin.router, prefix="/admin", dependencies=[Depends(require_admin)])`. That's handy when you include a router you don't own, or mount one router under two prefixes. Settings combine: prefixes concatenate, and tags and dependencies accumulate from app to router to route.

Routers can include other routers, so API versioning is just a `v1 = APIRouter(prefix="/v1")` that includes the feature routers, and the app includes `v1`.

Two habits keep larger codebases healthy. Keep imports flowing one way: routers import from `dependencies.py` and `models.py`, and `main.py` imports the routers; circular imports usually mean shared code lives in the wrong module. And keep handlers thin: parse input, call a plain service function, return a model. Business logic in plain functions can be tested without HTTP at all.
takeaways: APIRouter has the same decorators as the app; include it with app.include_router
prefix, tags and dependencies can be set on the router or at include time
Prefixes concatenate and dependencies accumulate down the tree
One router per feature module; keep imports flowing one way
pitfalls: Ending a prefix with a slash (prefix='/items/') and getting paths like /items//{id}.

quiz.q: router = APIRouter(prefix='/users') with @router.get('/{id}') is included with app.include_router(router, prefix='/v1'). What's the final path?
quiz.explain: The include-time prefix is prepended to the router's own prefix.

quiz.q: Where should a dependency that protects every admin route be declared?
options: On each admin endpoint, so it's explicit
Once, on the admin router or in its include_router call
quiz.explain: Router-level dependencies apply to every route in the router and can't be forgotten on a new endpoint.

concepts.name: Settings with pydantic-settings
concepts.summary: Load configuration from environment variables and .env files into a typed, validated Settings class.
concepts.why: The same image runs in dev, staging and production with different environment, and bad config fails at startup instead of mid-request.
concepts.body:
Hard-coded secrets and URLs are a classic production incident. The standard FastAPI answer is **pydantic-settings**, a separate package since Pydantic v2 (`pip install pydantic-settings`; `fastapi[standard]` doesn't include it). Subclass `BaseSettings` and declare typed fields with defaults:

- Each field is read from an environment variable of the same name, case-insensitively: `database_url` comes from `DATABASE_URL`.
- Values are validated and converted like any model: `debug: bool` accepts `1` or `true`, and `allowed_origins: list[str]` parses a JSON array string.
- `model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env", env_prefix="APP_")` also reads a `.env` file and namespaces the variables. Real environment variables win over the file.
- Fields without defaults are required. A missing `APP_SECRET_KEY` raises a validation error the moment `Settings()` is created, so the app fails fast instead of at the first login.
- `SecretStr` masks the value in logs and reprs; call `.get_secret_value()` when you really need it.

Expose settings through a dependency wrapped in `functools.lru_cache`, so the environment and `.env` file are read once rather than on every request:

```python
@lru_cache
def get_settings() -> Settings:
    return Settings()
```

Endpoints take `settings: Annotated[Settings, Depends(get_settings)]`, and tests swap values with `app.dependency_overrides[get_settings] = lambda: Settings(debug=True, secret_key="test")`. A module-level `settings = Settings()` also works and is common; the dependency version is easier to override and doesn't read the environment at import time.

Never commit `.env`. Commit a `.env.example` that lists every variable with a dummy value.
takeaways: BaseSettings fields come from environment variables (and optionally a .env file)
Values are validated; required fields without values fail at startup
Serve settings via an lru_cache'd dependency so tests can override them
Use SecretStr for secrets and never commit .env
pitfalls: Forgetting that pydantic-settings is a separate install; BaseSettings no longer lives in pydantic itself.

quiz.q: Settings has secret_key: str with no default and the variable isn't set. When does it fail?
options: Never; it defaults to an empty string
At the first request that reads it
When Settings() is instantiated, with a validation error
quiz.explain: Missing required fields fail validation as soon as the settings object is created.

quiz.q: Why wrap get_settings in @lru_cache?
options: So the settings are created, and the environment read, once instead of on every request
To encrypt secret values in memory
quiz.explain: Without the cache, every request would rebuild Settings and re-read the .env file.

concepts.name: Databases with SQLModel
concepts.summary: Define tables as SQLModel classes, get a session per request through a dependency, and run CRUD queries.
concepts.why: Most APIs are a thin layer over a database; getting sessions and models right avoids connection leaks and data exposure.
concepts.body:
FastAPI has no built-in database layer; you bring one. **SQLModel**, by FastAPI's author, fits most directly: a class can be both a Pydantic model and a SQLAlchemy table, so one definition gives you validation and persistence. Plain SQLAlchemy 2.0 with separate Pydantic schemas is equally common, and the session pattern is the same.

The moving parts:

- `create_engine(url)` once per process. The engine owns a connection pool. For SQLite with sync endpoints add `connect_args={"check_same_thread": False}`, because requests run on different threads.
- `SQLModel.metadata.create_all(engine)` creates the tables in demos; real projects use **Alembic** migrations.
- A **session dependency** that opens a `Session`, yields it to the endpoint, and closes it when the request is done. The `yield` makes it a dependency with cleanup code; the Advanced level explains exactly when that cleanup runs.

Queries use SQLAlchemy 2.0 style: `session.exec(select(Hero).where(Hero.age > 30).limit(10)).all()`, `session.get(Hero, hero_id)` for primary-key lookups, and `session.add(obj)`, `session.commit()`, `session.refresh(obj)` to insert and then load database-generated values such as the id.

Keep the separate-models discipline from the response models lesson. `table=True` marks the table class; `HeroCreate` and `HeroPublic` are plain data models for input and output, so clients can't set `id` and never see columns like `secret_name`. `Hero.model_validate(data)` turns validated input into a table row.

SQLModel and SQLAlchemy bind query values safely, so never build SQL strings from request data with f-strings. And when a lookup finds nothing, raise a 404 rather than returning `None`.
takeaways: One engine per process; one session per request via a yield dependency
table=True models map to tables; separate Create/Public models shape the API
add + commit + refresh to insert and read back generated ids
Use Alembic for schema changes in real projects
pitfalls: Creating a new engine per request, which throws away connection pooling.
Returning table objects without a response model and leaking internal columns.

quiz.q: Why does get_session use yield instead of return?
options: So the code after yield, closing the session, runs once the request has been handled
So one session is shared by all requests
quiz.explain: A yield dependency gets setup before the endpoint and teardown afterwards, like a context manager.

quiz.q: Why have HeroCreate and HeroPublic instead of using the Hero table class everywhere?
options: SQLModel table classes can't be used as parameters
So clients can't set server-owned fields like id or see columns like secret_name
Table classes are slower to serialize
quiz.explain: Separate input and output models define exactly what the API accepts and exposes.

concepts.name: Authentication: OAuth2 password flow and JWT
concepts.summary: Issue signed JWT access tokens from a /token endpoint and protect routes with an OAuth2PasswordBearer dependency.
concepts.why: Almost every API needs to know who is calling, and this is FastAPI's documented pattern, integrated with /docs.
concepts.body:
FastAPI's security utilities are dependencies that also describe themselves in OpenAPI, so `/docs` gets an Authorize button. The common setup is the **OAuth2 password flow** with **JWT** bearer tokens:

- The client POSTs form fields `username` and `password` to `/token`; `OAuth2PasswordRequestForm` parses them (form parsing needs `python-multipart`, included in `fastapi[standard]`).
- You verify the password against a stored **hash**, never plain text. FastAPI's docs use `pwdlib` with Argon2 via `PasswordHash.recommended()`.
- You return `{"access_token": token, "token_type": "bearer"}`, where the token is a JWT signed with a server secret using PyJWT.
- Later requests send `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. `OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="token")` is a dependency that extracts the token, or answers 401 if it's missing.
- Your `current_user` dependency decodes it (`jwt.decode` verifies the signature and the `exp` claim), loads the user, and raises 401 with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` on any failure.

Endpoints then just declare `user: Annotated[User, Depends(current_user)]`. Layer extra checks as further dependencies: one that rejects disabled accounts, another that requires an admin role.

A JWT is **signed, not encrypted**: anyone holding it can read the claims, so put only identifiers in it. Keep access tokens short-lived (15 to 60 minutes), keep the secret in settings, and always pass `algorithms=[...]` to `decode` so the token can't choose its own algorithm. Serve it only over HTTPS. If users sign in through Google or a corporate identity provider, you validate that provider's tokens instead, but the dependency shape stays the same.
takeaways: /token checks a password hash and returns a signed, expiring JWT
OAuth2PasswordBearer pulls the bearer token from the Authorization header
A current_user dependency verifies the token; endpoints just depend on it
JWTs are readable by anyone: sign, expire and keep secrets out of claims
pitfalls: Calling jwt.decode without algorithms=[...], or with verification options turned off.
Storing plain or fast-hashed (MD5, SHA-256) passwords instead of Argon2 or bcrypt.

quiz.q: Why must jwt.decode be given algorithms=['HS256']?
options: So the server, not the token header, decides which algorithm is acceptable
PyJWT can't detect the algorithm otherwise
quiz.explain: Pinning the algorithm blocks attacks where a forged token names a weaker or different algorithm.

quiz.q: A request to a route protected by OAuth2PasswordBearer has no Authorization header. What happens?
options: The token parameter is None and the endpoint runs
FastAPI responds 401 Not authenticated before the endpoint runs
FastAPI calls /token on the client's behalf
quiz.explain: The scheme dependency itself rejects requests without a bearer token.

concepts.name: Middleware and CORS
concepts.summary: Run code around every request with middleware, and let browser front ends on other origins call your API with CORSMiddleware.
concepts.why: Timing headers, request ids and CORS are cross-cutting concerns that belong in one place, not in every endpoint.
concepts.body:
**Middleware** wraps the whole application: it sees every request before any route runs and every response before it leaves. The quickest form is a decorator:

```python
@app.middleware("http")
async def add_timing(request: Request, call_next):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    response = await call_next(request)
    response.headers["X-Process-Time"] = f"{time.perf_counter() - start:.4f}"
    return response
```

`call_next` passes the request down the stack and returns the response. Middleware added later wraps the earlier ones, so the **last one added runs first** on the way in. Keep middleware for truly global concerns: request ids, timing, security headers, `GZipMiddleware`. Per-route logic belongs in dependencies, which see validated parameters and appear in the docs.

**CORS** (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is the middleware almost everyone needs. A page served from `https://app.example.com` calling `https://api.example.com` is cross-origin, and the browser won't let the page read the response unless the API answers with matching `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers. For requests with JSON bodies, custom headers or methods like PUT and DELETE, the browser first sends an `OPTIONS` **preflight**. `CORSMiddleware` handles all of it:

- `allow_origins`: exact origins, scheme + host + port, no path or trailing slash.
- `allow_credentials=True` if the browser sends cookies or Authorization headers. The CORS rules forbid a wildcard origin together with credentials, so list origins explicitly.
- `allow_methods` and `allow_headers` allow very little by default; `["*"]` is common.

CORS is a browser rule, not protection for your API: curl, scripts and servers ignore it entirely. Authentication still has to guard your endpoints.
concepts.code:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

app = FastAPI()
app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["https://app.example.com", "http://localhost:5173"],
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=["*"],
    allow_headers=["*"],
)

@app.get("/data")
def data():
    return {"ok": True}

c = TestClient(app)
pre = c.options("/data", headers={"Origin": "http://localhost:5173",
                                  "Access-Control-Request-Method": "GET"})
print(pre.status_code, pre.headers["access-control-allow-origin"])
# 200 http://localhost:5173
other = c.get("/data", headers={"Origin": "https://evil.example"})
print("access-control-allow-origin" in other.headers)
# False: the browser won't let that page read the response
takeaways: Middleware wraps every request; the last added runs first on the way in
Use middleware for global concerns, dependencies for per-route logic
CORSMiddleware answers preflights and adds Access-Control-Allow-* headers
CORS only constrains browsers; it is not authentication
pitfalls: Adding a trailing slash or path to an origin (https://app.example.com/), which never matches.

quiz.q: Your React app on http://localhost:5173 gets a CORS error calling your API, but the same request works with curl. Why?
options: The API only accepts curl's user agent
CORS is enforced by the browser, and the API isn't sending Access-Control-Allow-Origin for that origin
quiz.explain: Only browsers apply CORS; add the front end's origin to CORSMiddleware.

quiz.q: You call app.add_middleware(A) and then app.add_middleware(B). Which sees the request first?
quiz.explain: Each add_middleware wraps the existing stack, so the last one added is outermost.

concepts.name: Background tasks
concepts.summary: Schedule small jobs, like sending an email, to run after the response is sent, using the BackgroundTasks parameter.
concepts.why: Users shouldn't wait for a notification email or an audit log write before they get their response.
concepts.body:
Declare a parameter of type `BackgroundTasks` and FastAPI injects an instance. Call `background_tasks.add_task(func, *args, **kwargs)` and return as usual: the response goes out first, then the tasks run in the order they were added, in the same process. `func` can be a plain `def` (run in the thread pool) or an `async def` (run on the event loop).

`BackgroundTasks` also works in dependencies. A dependency can declare it and add tasks, and FastAPI merges everything into one list for the request, which suits things like "write an access log entry" inside an auth dependency.

Know the limits, because this is a convenience, not a job queue:

- Tasks live in memory. If the process restarts or crashes, pending tasks are lost, and nothing retries them.
- They run in the worker that served the request and share its resources. A heavy task slows that worker, and a blocking call inside an `async` task freezes its event loop.
- The client never learns whether a task succeeded; exceptions are only logged.

So use them for short, best-effort side effects: a notification, an audit record, a cache invalidation. For work that must happen, takes minutes, needs retries or should run on other machines, use a real queue (Celery, RQ, Dramatiq, Arq or a cloud queue): the endpoint enqueues a job and returns its id, often with status 202 Accepted.

Pass tasks plain values such as an email address or a row id, not request-scoped objects like the database session from a dependency. Open whatever the task needs, such as a fresh session, inside the task itself.
takeaways: Add a BackgroundTasks parameter and call add_task(func, *args)
Tasks run after the response is sent, in the same process
Dependencies can add tasks too; they're merged per request
Use a real queue for anything that must not be lost or needs retries
pitfalls: Passing the request's database session to a task instead of opening a new one inside it.

quiz.q: Your server restarts while 50 background tasks are still pending. What happens to them?
options: FastAPI persists them to disk first
They're lost, because BackgroundTasks keeps them in memory
quiz.explain: BackgroundTasks has no persistence or retry; use a job queue when that matters.

quiz.q: When do tasks added with add_task run?
options: In parallel with the endpoint function
After the response has been sent
At the start of the next request
quiz.explain: FastAPI sends the response first and then runs the tasks in order.

concepts.name: Testing with TestClient and pytest
concepts.summary: Call your app in-process with TestClient, swap dependencies with dependency_overrides, and assert on responses.
concepts.why: Fast, reliable API tests catch regressions in validation, auth and serialization before users do.
concepts.body:
`TestClient` (from `fastapi.testclient`, built on HTTPX) sends requests straight into your ASGI app with no server or network. It has the familiar `client.get`, `.post(json=...)`, `.put`, `.delete` methods, and each returns a response with `.status_code`, `.json()` and `.headers`. Tests are ordinary synchronous pytest functions, even when your endpoints are `async def`.

Use it as a context manager, `with TestClient(app) as client:`, when your app has a **lifespan**: entering runs startup and leaving runs shutdown. Without `with`, the lifespan never runs, and anything it creates is missing.

The real power is `app.dependency_overrides`, a dict that maps an original dependency to a replacement. Override `get_session` to use a test database, `current_user` to skip logging in, `get_settings` to flip a feature flag. Overrides are looked up on every request, so set them in a fixture and clear them afterwards with `app.dependency_overrides.clear()`, otherwise they leak into other tests.

What's worth testing:

- the happy path and the exact response shape (`assert r.json() == {...}`),
- validation: bad input returns 422,
- auth: no token gives 401, the wrong role 403,
- error mapping: missing resources give 404, and custom handlers produce their format,
- the schema: `client.get("/openapi.json")` returns 200, which catches models that can't be documented.

For a test database, SQLite in a temp file or a disposable Postgres container both work; the override pattern is the same. When a test itself must `await` things, such as async database setup, use `httpx.AsyncClient(transport=httpx.ASGITransport(app=app), base_url="http://test")` with an async test plugin like AnyIO's.
takeaways: TestClient calls the app in-process; tests stay synchronous
Use `with TestClient(app)` so lifespan startup and shutdown run
app.dependency_overrides swaps dependencies; clear it after each test
Test the error paths (401, 404, 422) as well as the happy path
pitfalls: Leaving dependency overrides in place between tests, so later tests pass or fail for the wrong reason.

quiz.q: Your app opens a connection pool in its lifespan, and tests fail with 'pool not initialized'. What's the likely fix?
options: Use `with TestClient(app) as client:` so lifespan startup runs
Call app.startup() at the top of each test
quiz.explain: TestClient only runs the lifespan when used as a context manager.

quiz.q: How do you make every request in a test act as user 'ann' without real tokens?
quiz.explain: Overriding the dependency replaces the whole authentication step for the test.

concepts.name: async def vs def and the threadpool
concepts.summary: How FastAPI runs async endpoints on the event loop and sync ones in a threadpool, and how to choose between them.
concepts.why: Choosing wrong can silently serialize a whole worker; it's the most common FastAPI performance bug.
concepts.body:
Each worker process runs one **event loop** (via Starlette and AnyIO). What happens to your function depends on how you declare it:

- `async def` runs **on the event loop**. While it waits at an `await`, the loop serves other requests. But a blocking call inside it, such as `time.sleep`, `requests.get`, a sync database driver or heavy computation, freezes the loop, and every request on that worker waits.
- Plain `def` runs in a **threadpool** via `run_in_threadpool`, so blocking I/O only ties up one thread. The same rules apply to dependencies.

The decision rule:

- The code awaits async libraries (`httpx.AsyncClient`, asyncpg, SQLAlchemy's asyncio extension, `redis.asyncio`): use `async def`.
- The code calls blocking libraries: use `def`.
- Trivial code with no I/O: either works, and `async def` skips the thread hop.

The threadpool is AnyIO's default limiter, **40 threads** per process. Under load with slow sync calls, requests queue for a free thread even though the CPU is idle. You can raise the limit at startup (`anyio.to_thread.current_default_thread_limiter().total_tokens = 100`), but threads cost memory and add contention; moving hot paths to async drivers usually scales further.

When an async endpoint must call one blocking function, push it off the loop with `await run_in_threadpool(fn, arg)` from `fastapi.concurrency`, or `await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(fn, arg)`. CPU-heavy work such as image processing doesn't belong in the web process at all: threads don't run Python bytecode in parallel under the GIL, so use a process pool or a task queue.

A quick diagnostic: if `/health` gets slow whenever one heavy endpoint is busy, something is blocking the event loop.
concepts.code:
import asyncio, time
import httpx
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/bad")
async def bad():
    time.sleep(0.5)            # blocks the event loop
    return "bad"

@app.get("/sync")
def sync():
    time.sleep(0.5)            # runs in the threadpool
    return "ok"

@app.get("/async")
async def non_blocking():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.5)   # yields to the loop while waiting
    return "ok"

async def main():
    transport = httpx.ASGITransport(app=app)
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(transport=transport, base_url="http://t") as c:
        for path in ("/bad", "/sync", "/async"):
            start = time.perf_counter()
            await asyncio.gather(*(c.get(path) for _ in range(5)))
            print(path, round(time.perf_counter() - start, 1))

asyncio.run(main())   # /bad 2.5   /sync 0.5   /async 0.5
takeaways: async def runs on the event loop: never block inside it
def runs in a 40-thread pool: safe for blocking libraries
Use run_in_threadpool to call one blocking function from async code
CPU-bound work belongs in processes or a task queue, not the web worker
pitfalls: Calling requests, time.sleep or a sync DB driver inside async def.
Making everything async def 'for speed' while still using blocking libraries.

quiz.q: An async def endpoint calls requests.get(), which takes 2 s. Ten requests arrive at once on one worker. What happens?
options: All finish in about 2 s because the endpoint is async
FastAPI detects the blocking call and moves it to a thread
They run one after another, about 20 s in total, because the event loop is blocked
The requests fail with a timeout error immediately
quiz.explain: A blocking call inside async def holds the loop, so the other requests can't progress.

quiz.q: What's the smallest correct fix for that endpoint?
options: Change it to a plain def so it runs in the threadpool
quiz.explain: A def endpoint runs in a worker thread, where blocking only occupies that thread.

concepts.name: Dependencies with yield and scopes
concepts.summary: Use yield in dependencies for setup and teardown, handle exceptions in them, and control when teardown runs with scope.
concepts.why: Sessions, transactions, locks and file handles need reliable cleanup, including when the endpoint raises.
concepts.body:
A dependency that **yields** works like a context manager: code before `yield` is setup, the yielded value is injected, and code after `yield` is teardown. FastAPI wraps it with `contextlib.contextmanager` (or `asynccontextmanager` for `async def`) and enters it on an exit stack, so teardowns run in reverse order of setup. Sync generator dependencies run both halves in the threadpool.

Exceptions flow into the dependency: if the endpoint or a later dependency raises, the exception is re-raised at the `yield`. That enables a transaction pattern:

```python
def get_tx_session():
    with Session(engine) as session:
        try:
            yield session
            session.commit()
        except Exception:
            session.rollback()
            raise
```

Always re-raise in an `except` block, or raise a new `HTTPException`. If you swallow the exception, the client still gets a 500 but nothing is logged, which is miserable to debug. Raising `HTTPException` *before* the `yield` is fine too, for example when a lock can't be acquired.

**When** does teardown run? Since FastAPI 0.118 the default, `scope="request"`, runs it after the response has been sent, so the resource stays alive while a `StreamingResponse` streams. (From 0.106 to 0.117 it ran before sending.) The catch: a commit after `yield` happens after the client already received its 200, so a failing commit can't change the response. Two fixes:

- commit explicitly in the endpoint before returning, or
- since 0.121, declare `Depends(get_tx_session, scope="function")`, which runs teardown as soon as the endpoint function returns, before the response is sent.

A `"function"`-scoped dependency may depend on `"request"`-scoped ones but not the reverse, because outer resources must outlive inner ones.
takeaways: Code before yield is setup, after yield is teardown, in reverse order
Exceptions from the endpoint are re-raised at the yield: always re-raise
Default scope='request' tears down after the response is sent (0.118+)
scope='function' (0.121+) tears down before the response, so commit errors can still fail the request
pitfalls: Catching an exception after yield and not re-raising it, which hides the error from logs.

quiz.q: With the default scope, a dependency commits after yield and the commit fails. What has the client already received?
options: Nothing; the response waits for the commit
The successful response, because teardown runs after it was sent
quiz.explain: Request-scoped teardown runs after sending, so its errors can't change the response.

quiz.q: Which dependency arrangement is invalid?
options: A plain return-style dependency inside a yield dependency
A scope='function' dependency depending on a scope='request' one
Two scope='request' dependencies depending on each other in a chain
A scope='request' dependency depending on a scope='function' one
quiz.explain: A request-scoped resource outlives the function scope, so it can't rely on something already torn down.

concepts.name: Lifespan: startup and shutdown
concepts.summary: Create shared resources such as connection pools, HTTP clients or ML models once per process with a lifespan context manager.
concepts.why: Opening a client or loading a model per request is slow and leaks resources; per-process setup belongs in lifespan.
concepts.body:
Some things should exist once per process, not once per request: a database engine, an `httpx.AsyncClient`, a Redis pool, a loaded ML model. FastAPI's tool for this is **lifespan**: an async context manager passed to `FastAPI(lifespan=...)`. Code before its `yield` runs at startup, before the server accepts requests; code after it runs at shutdown, once requests have stopped.

Lifespan replaces the deprecated `@app.on_event("startup")` and `@app.on_event("shutdown")` handlers. Don't mix them: when you pass `lifespan`, `on_event` handlers aren't called.

Where to keep the resources? Module globals work, but **lifespan state** is cleaner: yield a dict, `yield {"http": client}`, and each request can read it as `request.state.http` (every request gets a shallow copy of that dict). Wrap the lookup in a dependency so endpoints stay simple and tests can override it:

```python
def get_http(request: Request) -> httpx.AsyncClient:
    return request.state.http
```

Things to keep in mind:

- Each worker process runs its own lifespan. Four workers mean four pools, so size them accordingly.
- If startup raises, the server doesn't start. That's good: fail fast on bad configuration or an unreachable database.
- Only the main app's lifespan runs, not those of sub-applications mounted with `app.mount`.
- In tests, lifespan runs only inside `with TestClient(app) as client:`.

Clean up in reverse order of creation, and put the cleanup after `yield` in a `try/finally` if you open several resources, or use `contextlib.AsyncExitStack`.
concepts.code:
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from typing import Annotated
import httpx
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    client = httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=5)
    print("startup: client created")
    yield {"http": client}          # becomes request.state.http
    await client.aclose()
    print("shutdown: client closed")

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)

def get_http(request: Request) -> httpx.AsyncClient:
    return request.state.http

@app.get("/client")
async def which_client(http: Annotated[httpx.AsyncClient, Depends(get_http)]):
    return {"closed": http.is_closed}

with TestClient(app) as c:              # runs startup ... shutdown
    print(c.get("/client").json())      # {'closed': False}
takeaways: lifespan = async context manager: before yield is startup, after is shutdown
Yield a dict to expose resources as request.state.<name>
Each worker process runs its own lifespan
Use lifespan instead of the deprecated on_event handlers
pitfalls: Creating an httpx.AsyncClient or DB engine inside each request instead of once in lifespan.

quiz.q: You run the app with 4 workers and the lifespan creates a DB pool of 10 connections. How many connections can the app open?
options: 40, since each worker runs its own lifespan
quiz.explain: Workers are separate processes, each with its own lifespan and pool.

quiz.q: Where do resources yielded from lifespan as a dict show up?
options: As request.state attributes in each request
quiz.explain: Lifespan state is copied into each request's state.

concepts.name: Uploads, file and streaming responses
concepts.summary: Accept uploads with UploadFile, send files with FileResponse, and stream generated data with StreamingResponse.
concepts.why: Files and large or slow-to-produce responses would exhaust memory or time out if handled as one JSON blob.
concepts.body:
**Uploads** arrive as `multipart/form-data` (parsed by `python-multipart`, part of `fastapi[standard]`). Declare `file: UploadFile` and you get `filename`, `content_type`, `size` and a spooled temporary file: kept in memory up to a threshold, then on disk, so large uploads don't eat RAM. Read it with `await file.read(size)` in chunks, or use the sync `file.file` object. A `bytes` parameter (with `File()`) loads everything into memory, so keep it for small files.

Combine files with `Form()` fields, and use `list[UploadFile]` for several files. A multipart request can't also carry a JSON body, so metadata travels as form fields. `filename` and `content_type` come from the client: never use the filename as a path, and enforce size and type limits yourself.

**Sending files**: `FileResponse(path, media_type=..., filename="report.pdf")` streams the file from disk in chunks and sets `Content-Disposition` so browsers download it under that name.

**Streaming**: `StreamingResponse(iterator, media_type=...)` sends whatever a sync or async generator yields as it's produced, which suits CSV exports, proxying an upstream download or LLM tokens. It bypasses response models, so you serialize each chunk yourself. Newer releases add built-ins: from 0.134 a path operation can itself `yield` items to stream JSON Lines, and from 0.135 `response_class=EventSourceResponse` (from `fastapi.sse`) streams Server-Sent Events.

Streaming interacts with resources: with the default dependency scope (0.118+), a database session from a `yield` dependency stays open until streaming finishes. That's what you want if the generator reads from it, and wasteful if it doesn't.
takeaways: UploadFile spools to disk and exposes filename, content_type and size
Files and Form() fields go together; JSON bodies don't mix with multipart
FileResponse sends files from disk; StreamingResponse sends generator output
Validate size and type yourself; client-supplied metadata isn't trustworthy
pitfalls: Using the uploaded filename directly as a path on disk (path traversal).

quiz.q: Why is UploadFile usually better than a bytes parameter for uploads?
options: UploadFile spools large files to disk instead of holding everything in memory
UploadFile validates the file type automatically
quiz.explain: A bytes parameter reads the entire upload into memory; UploadFile uses a spooled temp file.

quiz.q: An endpoint needs a file plus metadata. How should the client send the metadata?
options: As a JSON body next to the file
As form fields in the same multipart request
quiz.explain: A request has one body; with multipart, extra data travels as form fields.

concepts.name: WebSockets
concepts.summary: Hold long-lived two-way connections with @app.websocket, handle disconnects, and know the limits of in-process broadcasting.
concepts.why: Chat, live dashboards and collaborative editing need the server to push messages without the client polling.
concepts.body:
A WebSocket starts as an HTTP request and is then upgraded to a persistent two-way channel. Declare an endpoint with `@app.websocket("/ws/{room}")` and an `async def` that takes a `WebSocket`:

- `await websocket.accept()` completes the handshake. Until you accept, you can still reject the connection.
- `receive_text()`, `receive_json()` and `receive_bytes()` wait for the next message; `send_text()`, `send_json()` and `send_bytes()` push one.
- When the client goes away, the next receive raises `WebSocketDisconnect`. Catch it to clean up, such as removing the connection from a room.

Path and query parameters, `Depends` and `Annotated` work as usual. Authentication needs care: browsers can't set custom headers like `Authorization` on a WebSocket, so pass a token as a query parameter or rely on a cookie. To refuse, raise `WebSocketException(code=status.WS_1008_POLICY_VIOLATION)`; `HTTPException` doesn't apply once you're talking WebSocket.

Each open connection is a coroutine parked on `await`, so thousands are cheap, provided you never block the loop. Use async libraries throughout.

The classic "connection manager" that keeps a list of sockets and loops over them to broadcast only works **within one process**. With several workers or replicas, a user connected to worker A never sees messages sent from worker B. For real fan-out, publish through Redis pub/sub, NATS, Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY or a managed service, with each worker forwarding to its own sockets.

In production, make sure your proxy or load balancer passes the `Upgrade` headers and that idle timeouts are longer than your ping interval. Test WebSockets with `TestClient.websocket_connect`.
takeaways: @app.websocket + await websocket.accept() opens the channel
WebSocketDisconnect signals the client left: clean up there
Authenticate with a query token or cookie; reject with WebSocketException
In-memory broadcasting only reaches clients on the same process
pitfalls: Shipping an in-memory connection manager to a multi-worker deployment and losing messages between workers.

quiz.q: Your chat app runs with 4 Uvicorn workers and uses a list of connections in memory to broadcast. What goes wrong?
options: Every message is delivered four times
Users only receive messages from users connected to the same worker
WebSockets can't run with multiple workers
quiz.explain: Each worker is a separate process with its own list; cross-worker fan-out needs a broker such as Redis.

quiz.q: How should a browser client authenticate a WebSocket connection?
options: By sending HTTP Basic credentials after accept
With a token in the query string or a cookie, checked before accepting
With an Authorization header set in JavaScript
quiz.explain: The browser WebSocket API can't add custom headers, so tokens travel as a query parameter or cookie.

concepts.name: Customizing OpenAPI
concepts.summary: Document extra responses, examples and tags, control operation ids for client generation, and post-process the schema.
concepts.why: A precise schema is what client SDKs, API gateways and partner teams are built on, so it deserves the same care as code.
concepts.body:
The generated schema is good by default; a few knobs make it excellent.

**Extra responses.** FastAPI only knows the success response and the 422. Document the rest with `responses={404: {"model": Message, "description": "Item not found"}}` on a decorator or router, so clients know the error shapes.

**Examples.** `Field(examples=[...])` on model fields, or `model_config = {"json_schema_extra": {"examples": [...]}}` for a whole model, appear in the JSON Schema. `Body(openapi_examples={...})` adds named examples that Swagger UI shows in a dropdown.

**Organization.** Tag every operation, and describe tags with `FastAPI(openapi_tags=[{"name": "items", "description": "..."}])`, which also fixes their order. Hide internal endpoints with `include_in_schema=False`.

**Operation ids.** Client generators turn each `operationId` into a method name. The defaults are long (`read_item_items__item_id__get`), so pass `generate_unique_id_function` to `FastAPI()` to build names like `items-read_item` from the route's tag and function name. They must stay unique.

**Input vs output schemas.** With Pydantic v2, a model with defaults can produce separate `Item-Input` and `Item-Output` schemas, because output fields with defaults are always present. That's accurate; if your tooling dislikes it, `FastAPI(separate_input_output_schemas=False)` merges them.

**Post-processing.** For anything else, replace `app.openapi` with a function that calls `fastapi.openapi.utils.get_openapi(...)`, edits the dict (add a logo, security schemes, vendor extensions) and caches it in `app.openapi_schema`, so it's built once rather than on every request.
takeaways: responses={code: {...}} documents error shapes beyond 200 and 422
Field examples and Body openapi_examples improve the docs
generate_unique_id_function gives client SDKs clean method names
Override app.openapi and cache in app.openapi_schema for anything else
pitfalls: Overriding app.openapi without caching the result, so the schema is regenerated on every request.

quiz.q: Generated TypeScript client methods have names like read_item_items__item_id__get. What fixes this at the source?
options: A generate_unique_id_function on the FastAPI app
quiz.explain: Operation ids come from that function; returning tag + name gives short, stable method names.

quiz.q: Why might one model appear as Item-Input and Item-Output in the schema?
options: Fields with defaults are optional in requests but always present in responses
quiz.explain: Pydantic v2 describes input and output modes separately when they differ.

concepts.name: Deployment: workers, proxies and containers
concepts.summary: Run FastAPI in production with fastapi run or Uvicorn, choose worker counts, sit behind a proxy and package it in Docker.
concepts.why: Development defaults (one process, auto-reload, localhost) are wrong for production in ways that cost uptime and performance.
concepts.body:
In production run the app with `fastapi run` (or `uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0`), never with `--reload`.

**Workers.** One Uvicorn process uses one CPU core for Python code. `fastapi run --workers 4` starts a manager with four worker processes, each with its own event loop, memory, threadpool and lifespan. On a VM, start near one worker per core and measure. On **Kubernetes** or similar, run a single process per container and scale with replicas instead; the orchestrator already does process management, health checks and restarts. Gunicorn with Uvicorn workers is a common older setup that's no longer necessary.

**Behind a proxy.** TLS usually terminates at a load balancer or reverse proxy, which forwards plain HTTP. For correct client IPs, `https` URLs and redirects, the server must trust `X-Forwarded-*` headers: `--proxy-headers` (on by default with `fastapi run`) plus `--forwarded-allow-ips` listing the proxy's addresses. If the proxy serves the app under a path prefix like `/api`, set `--root-path /api` so the docs and generated URLs include it.

**Containers.** Copy and install requirements before copying your code so Docker caches the dependency layer, and use the exec form of `CMD` so the server is PID 1 and receives `SIGTERM` for a graceful shutdown.

**Operational basics.**

- Configuration through environment variables (the settings lesson).
- A cheap `/health` endpoint for liveness and one that checks dependencies for readiness.
- Database migrations as a separate deploy step, not inside every worker's startup.
- Logs to stdout, collected by the platform.
concepts.code:
# Dockerfile
FROM python:3.13-slim

WORKDIR /code
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

# dependencies first: this layer is cached until requirements.txt changes
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY ./app ./app

# exec form: the server is PID 1 and gets SIGTERM for graceful shutdown
# one process per container; scale with replicas (or add --workers on a VM)
# behind a proxy, also pass: "--forwarded-allow-ips", "<proxy IPs>"
CMD ["fastapi", "run", "app/main.py", "--port", "80"]

# docker build -t myapi . && docker run -p 8000:80 --env-file .env myapi
takeaways: Production: fastapi run / uvicorn without --reload
--workers N for VMs; one process per container on Kubernetes
Behind a proxy, trust X-Forwarded-* headers only from the proxy and set root_path for prefixes
Docker: install deps before copying code, exec-form CMD
pitfalls: Trusting forwarded headers from everyone (--forwarded-allow-ips '*') on a server that's directly reachable from the internet.

quiz.q: You deploy to Kubernetes. What's the usual recommendation for Uvicorn workers?
options: Use --reload so pods pick up new code
Run Gunicorn with 2 x cores + 1 workers
As many workers as CPU cores in every container
One process per container, scaled with replicas
quiz.explain: The orchestrator handles replication and restarts, so each container runs a single process.

quiz.q: Behind an HTTPS load balancer, your redirects point to http:// URLs. What's missing?
options: Trusting the proxy's X-Forwarded-Proto header (proxy headers plus forwarded-allow-ips)
quiz.explain: Without trusting forwarded headers, the app thinks requests arrived over plain HTTP.

concepts.name: Under the hood: ASGI and Starlette
concepts.summary: How an ASGI server calls your app with scope, receive and send, and how FastAPI layers its middleware stack and router on Starlette.
concepts.why: Debugging middleware order, streaming, 500s without CORS headers or performance means knowing what actually runs per request.
concepts.body:
**ASGI** is the interface between servers and Python async apps. An ASGI app is just `async def app(scope, receive, send)`. Uvicorn parses the HTTP bytes and calls it once per connection or request:

- `scope` is a dict describing the connection: `type` (`"http"`, `"websocket"` or `"lifespan"`), `method`, `path`, `query_string`, and `headers` as a list of `(bytes, bytes)` pairs.
- `await receive()` returns events such as `{"type": "http.request", "body": b"...", "more_body": False}`; bodies may arrive in chunks.
- `await send(...)` emits `http.response.start` (status and headers) and then one or more `http.response.body` messages, which is how streaming works.

`FastAPI` subclasses Starlette's application. On the first request it builds the middleware stack, outermost first: `ServerErrorMiddleware` (turns uncaught exceptions into 500s and runs your `Exception` handler), your middleware in reverse order of adding, `ExceptionMiddleware` (`HTTPException` and your other handlers), FastAPI's exit-stack middleware, then the **router**. The router tries routes in order; the matching `APIRoute` reads the body, solves dependencies, calls your function and serializes the result.

That layout explains real surprises:

- A 500 is produced *outside* your middleware, so it carries no CORS headers and the browser reports a CORS error instead of the crash.
- `@app.middleware("http")` is built on `BaseHTTPMiddleware`, which wraps each request in extra tasks and streams; it's convenient but adds overhead. Hot-path middleware is better written as pure ASGI, as in the example, wrapping `send` to edit headers.
- Anything ASGI can be mounted: `app.mount("/static", StaticFiles(directory="static"))`, another FastAPI app, or a WSGI app via an adapter.

Starlette's `Request` is a thin, lazy view over `scope` and `receive`.
concepts.code:
import time
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from starlette.types import ASGIApp, Message, Receive, Scope, Send

class TimingMiddleware:                      # pure ASGI: no BaseHTTPMiddleware
    def __init__(self, app: ASGIApp) -> None:
        self.app = app

    async def __call__(self, scope: Scope, receive: Receive, send: Send) -> None:
        if scope["type"] != "http":           # pass websocket/lifespan through
            return await self.app(scope, receive, send)
        start = time.perf_counter()

        async def send_wrapper(message: Message) -> None:
            if message["type"] == "http.response.start":
                ms = f"{(time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000:.1f}"
                message["headers"] = [*message["headers"], (b"server-timing", f"app;dur={ms}".encode())]
            await send(message)

        await self.app(scope, receive, send_wrapper)

app = FastAPI()
app.add_middleware(TimingMiddleware)

@app.get("/")
def root():
    return {"ok": True}

print(TestClient(app).get("/").headers["server-timing"])   # app;dur=0.9 (varies)
takeaways: An ASGI app is async (scope, receive, send); responses are sent as messages
Stack: ServerErrorMiddleware > your middleware > ExceptionMiddleware > router
500 responses bypass user middleware, so they lack CORS and custom headers
Pure ASGI middleware avoids BaseHTTPMiddleware's overhead
pitfalls: Reading the request body in BaseHTTPMiddleware and expecting streaming endpoints to behave normally.

quiz.q: A browser shows a CORS error, but the server log shows an unhandled exception. Why does the error look like CORS?
options: The 500 is generated by ServerErrorMiddleware outside CORSMiddleware, so it has no CORS headers
Browsers always report 500s as CORS errors
The exception happened inside the preflight
CORSMiddleware converts exceptions into CORS errors
quiz.explain: The outermost error middleware builds the 500 after the CORS layer has been unwound.

quiz.q: In ASGI, how does a server send a streamed response?
options: One http.response.start message followed by several http.response.body messages with more_body=True
By returning a generator from the app
quiz.explain: The body is a sequence of send() messages, the last with more_body False.

concepts.name: How the dependency resolver works
